Where Your Money Goes: Value Chains, Market Channels and Your Real Costs

Before you change how you sell, you need a clear picture of who handles your crop after it leaves your farm, which buyers exist besides the first one at your gate, and what each bag or basket actually costs you to produce. This module gives you those three pictures, with numbers you can work out on your phone.
From Harvest to Plate: Mapping the Value Chain for Your Crop
Name the main actors in a farm produce value chain and the job each one does
Explain why the price rises at each step and which costs and risks sit behind that rise
Draw a simple value chain map for one crop you grow
Identify one step where you could keep more of the final value

Every crop you sell travels a road before someone eats it. A basket of tomatoes picked in a farm near Zaria may pass through four or five pairs of hands before it reaches a pot of stew in Lagos. Each person along that road does some work, carries some risk and takes a share of the final price. This road, with all its people and their jobs, is called the **value chain**.

Agribusiness simply means treating farming as a business that runs from the field to the buyer, not only as growing. Market access means being able to reach buyers who pay a fair price for what you have, with enough information to choose between them. Both start with knowing your value chain.
The usual actors in a Nigerian produce chain
list
**Farmer (producer):** grows, harvests and often does the first drying, shelling or sorting.
**Assembler or aggregator:** buys small amounts from many farmers, often at the farm gate or village market, and gathers them into a truckload. Sometimes called a middleman or agent.
**Wholesaler:** buys in bulk, usually at a big urban or border market, and sells on to retailers and processors.
**Processor:** turns raw produce into another product, for example a feed mill using maize, a tomato paste factory, or a woman frying garri from cassava.
**Retailer:** sells small quantities to households, from a market stall, kiosk or supermarket.
**Consumer:** the household or restaurant that finally buys and eats it.

Why the price rises at each step

It is easy to think the middleman simply steals the difference between your price and the market price. Sometimes margins really are unfair, especially when the farmer has no other buyer and no price information. But much of the gap pays for real costs: hiring a truck, loading and offloading, market and road levies, the trader's time, money tied up for days, and **losses**. Fresh produce bruises, rots and gets crushed on the way. A trader who loses one basket in six must charge more on the five that arrive.
example
Worked example: where the money goes on 40 baskets of tomatoes
For example, Hauwa sells 40 raffia baskets of tomatoes at her farm gate to an aggregator. These are illustrative numbers to show the method, not today's prices.
Hauwa receives ₦12,000 per basket: 40 × ₦12,000 = ₦480,000.
The aggregator pays transport to the city market of about ₦2,500 per basket: 40 × ₦2,500 = ₦100,000.
Loading, offloading and levies cost about ₦500 per basket: 40 × ₦500 = ₦20,000.
Total cost to the aggregator: ₦480,000 + ₦100,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦600,000.
On the way, 6 baskets are crushed or spoil in the heat, so only 34 baskets are sold.
His margin: ₦748,000 − ₦600,000 = ₦148,000, before his own time and the risk of a bad market day.

The city price is almost double the farm gate price, but most of the gap is transport, levies and lost baskets. Hauwa's best levers are cutting losses, sorting better tomatoes for a better price, and selling with others in bulk so that she can share in some of that margin herself.

How to map your own chain
steps
Pick one crop that brings you the most money, for example maize, tomatoes, yam, soybeans or pepper.
Write down who bought it from you last season, the unit (bag, basket, tuber, kg) and the price you received.
Ask that buyer, politely, where the produce goes next. Many traders will tell you the market or the mill.
Visit or phone someone at the next step and ask what they pay for the same unit and quality.
Note the main costs between the two steps: transport, levies, bags, losses, waiting time.
Draw the chain on paper with the price written under each actor.
callout
Use your phone to collect prices

A short WhatsApp voice note to a relative who trades in a bigger market, or a call to your state Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension office, can give you a recent price. Write the date beside every price you collect, because farm prices change from week to week.
Where farmers can capture more value

Once your map is on paper, look for steps that a farmer, or a group of farmers, could do themselves. The common ones are: **sorting and grading** so the best produce earns a better price; **better packaging** such as plastic crates or clean new bags, which cut losses; **storage** so you are not forced to sell when prices are lowest; **bulking** with other farmers to fill a truck and reach a wholesaler or processor directly; and **simple processing** where it makes sense. You will practise each of these later in the course.
Do not try to cut out everyone

Traders provide transport, cash on the spot and buyers you may not know. The goal is not to remove them but to have choices, information and better quality, so that you negotiate from strength instead of accepting the first price.
A value chain is the road your crop travels from your farm to the consumer, with a price at each step.
Much of the gap between farm gate and city price pays for transport, levies and losses, not only profit.

Grading, better packaging, storage and selling in bulk are the main farmer-level levers.

Comparing Market Channels: Farm Gate, Rural Market, Wholesale, Processor and Institutional Buyers
Describe five common market channels for farm produce in Nigeria

A **market channel** is the route you choose to sell through. Most smallholder farmers use one channel by habit: the trader who comes to the farm. That is not wrong, but if it is your only option, you have no bargaining power. This lesson shows you how to compare channels properly, using the price you actually keep, not the price you hear about.

Compare the net price, not the offered price

The **offered price** is what a buyer says they will pay. The **net price** is what you keep after the costs of selling through that channel: transport, loading, levies, bags, and any produce they reject. Always convert offers to the same unit, for example naira per 100 kg bag or naira per kg, before you compare.
Worked example: three offers for 20 bags of maize
For example, Blessing in Niger State has 20 bags of shelled maize, each weighed at 100 kg. The prices below are illustrative, not current market prices.
Farm gate offer: ₦55,000 per bag, no costs. Net = 20 × ₦55,000 = ₦1,100,000.
Weekly market: ₦62,000 per bag. Transport ₦1,500, levy ₦300 and loading ₦200 per bag = ₦2,000. Net per bag = ₦60,000. Net total = 20 × ₦60,000 = ₦1,200,000.
Feed mill: ₦66,000 per bag, but transport to the mill is ₦3,000 per bag. Net per bag = ₦63,000.
The mill rejects 2 bags for high moisture. Blessing sells those 2 at the farm gate later for ₦50,000 each because they are lower quality.
Payment from the mill arrives 14 days after delivery.

The mill gives the best net total (₦1,234,000), about ₦134,000 more than the farm gate. But Blessing must dry her maize properly to avoid rejection, and she must be able to wait two weeks for the money. If school fees are due tomorrow, the weekly market at ₦1,200,000 with same-day cash may suit her better.
Questions to ask before choosing a channel
What exact quality do they want (moisture, size, colour, cleanliness, ripeness)?
What is the minimum quantity, and do they collect or must I deliver?
How do they weigh or measure, and can I watch the weighing?
When and how do they pay: cash, bank transfer, or after an invoice?
What happens to produce they reject?
Will they buy again next season, and on what terms?
delivery-truck
A delivery truck on the road
Transport is often the biggest cost between channels, so include it in every comparison.
Unknown buyers and payment

When you sell to a new buyer, agree payment terms before loading. Do not release produce on the strength of an SMS credit alert or a screenshot; open your own bank or mobile money app (for example Opay or Moniepoint) and confirm the money has actually arrived. Fake alerts are a common trick.
Two more routes to consider

Beyond the five main channels, two other routes are growing. The first is **selling directly to households, food sellers and restaurants** through WhatsApp: you post what you have, with photos and a price per kg, and deliver to nearby buyers. It suits small volumes of fresh or cleaned produce and gives a retail price, but delivery takes time. The second is an **outgrower or contract farming scheme**, where a processor agrees before planting to buy your crop at harvest, sometimes supplying seed or fertiliser on credit that is deducted from your payment. Read such contracts carefully: check the price formula, the quality rules and how input costs are deducted before you sign.

You do not have to move all your produce to a new channel at once. A sensible approach is to keep your usual buyer for most of the harvest and test a second channel with a smaller share, for example a quarter. Record the net price from both, and use what you learn to decide next season. Having a second real option also strengthens your position when your usual buyer names a price.
A market channel is the route you sell through; most farmers rely on just one by habit.

Know Your Numbers: Cost of Production per Unit and Your Readiness Check
List every cost that goes into producing one season's crop, including your own labour
Calculate your cost of production per bag and per kilogram
Use your cost per unit to set a minimum acceptable selling price
Assess your readiness for better market access with a short checklist

You cannot tell whether a price is good if you do not know what the crop cost you to grow. Many farmers know roughly what they spent on fertiliser, but forget the ploughing, the empty bags, the hired hands for shelling or the land rent. **Cost of production per unit** is the total cost of the season divided by the number of units you harvested. It is the single most useful number in this course.
What to include
**Land:** rent, or what you could earn by renting it out if it is yours.
**Land preparation:** clearing, ploughing, harrowing, ridging.
**Inputs:** seed, fertiliser, herbicide, insecticide, manure.
**Labour:** hired workers for planting, weeding, spraying, harvesting, shelling. Also give a value to your own and your family's days, using the local daily wage.
**Post-harvest:** drying tarpaulins, threshing or shelling, empty bags, storage bags, transport from farm to home or store.
**Other:** loan interest, cooperative dues, equipment repairs.
Worked example: cost per bag for one hectare of maize
For example, Amina farms one hectare of maize in Kaduna State. These figures are illustrative to show the method; use your own records.
Land rent ₦50,000; land preparation ₦90,000; seed ₦45,000.
Fertiliser ₦300,000; herbicide and spraying ₦60,000.
Hired labour for planting, weeding and fertiliser application ₦150,000.
Harvest, shelling and drying ₦120,000; empty bags and transport home ₦35,000.
Harvest: 25 bags of 100 kg. Cost per bag = ₦850,000 ÷ 25 = ₦34,000. Cost per kg = ₦34,000 ÷ 100 = ₦340.
Amina wants at least a 20% margin on cost: ₦34,000 × 1.20 = ₦40,800 per bag minimum.

Any offer below ₦34,000 per bag means Amina loses money. Between ₦34,000 and ₦40,800 she covers costs but earns less than her target. Now, when a trader offers ₦38,000, she knows exactly what that means for her household.
Yield changes everything

If Amina's harvest had been 17 bags instead of 25, her cost per bag would be ₦850,000 ÷ 17 = ₦50,000, nearly half as much again. Good agronomy and lower post-harvest losses lower your cost per unit just as surely as a higher price raises your income.
Turn cost into a minimum price
Add up all costs for the season for one crop.
Count or weigh the harvest in the unit you sell (bag, basket, kg, tuber).
Divide total cost by total units to get cost per unit.
Multiply by 1 plus your target margin (for example 1.20 for 20%) to get your minimum selling price.
Compare every offer with these two numbers: cost per unit and minimum price.

Variable and fixed costs

**Variable costs** go up or down with how much you produce: seed, fertiliser, hired labour, bags and transport. **Fixed costs** stay about the same whatever you produce in a season, for example a knapsack sprayer, repairs to your store or yearly group dues. Fixed costs bought for several seasons should be spread out: a sprayer that lasts four seasons counts as one quarter of its price each season. Because fixed costs are shared across all your units, a bigger, healthier harvest lowers the fixed cost carried by each bag.
Common costing mistakes
Counting only the cash spent and forgetting family labour, land and borrowed tools.
Leaving out post-harvest costs such as shelling, bags, tarpaulins and transport home.
Using an estimated harvest instead of the weighed or counted harvest.
Putting all costs on one crop when two crops shared the land; split shared costs, for example by the share of the land each crop used.
Forgetting loan interest or the fees on a savings group loan.
Keep receipts in one place
Use a small notebook or a WhatsApp chat with yourself to record each farm expense with its date the day you spend it. At the end of the season, adding them up takes minutes instead of guesswork.

Adding Value After Harvest: Handling, Quality, Records and Measured Gains

Most of the extra money a farmer can earn is won or lost in the days after harvest. This module covers drying, cleaning, grading and packing, the food safety and quality standards buyers check, and the simple records that prove whether your changes actually raised your income.
Post-Harvest Handling: Drying, Cleaning, Grading and Packing
Dry grain properly and check moisture with the salt-in-a-bottle test
Clean and sort produce into clear grades that buyers recognise
Choose packaging that reduces losses for grain and for fresh produce
Calculate whether grading pays after the extra labour

Post-harvest handling is everything you do between cutting the crop and handing it to the buyer. Done carelessly, it causes mould, insect damage, bruising and weight loss. Done well, it gives you produce that buyers trust and pay more for. The steps differ for dry crops such as maize, sorghum, soybeans and rice, and for fresh crops such as tomatoes, pepper and leafy vegetables, so we look at both.
Post-harvest steps for grain
Harvest at maturity
Dry well
Thresh and clean
Grade
Bag and label
Store safely
Each step protects quality; skipping drying or cleaning undoes the work of every step after it.
Drying grain properly

Wet grain is the root of most storage problems. It heats up, grows mould and attracts insects. For maize, a moisture content of about **13% or lower** is the level usually recommended for safe storage, and many buyers such as feed mills test for it. Dry on a clean tarpaulin or raised platform, never on bare earth or along the roadside, where grain picks up stones, dirt and contamination and where drying spreads mould from the soil. Spread it thinly, turn it several times a day, and cover it at night and when rain threatens.
The salt-in-a-bottle moisture test
Take a clean, completely dry glass bottle or jar with a lid.
Fill it about one third with grain taken from several places in the heap.
Add two to three tablespoons of dry table salt.
Close the lid and shake well for about two minutes, then let it rest for about fifteen minutes.
Shake again and look: if salt sticks to the inside of the jar, the grain is still too wet to store. Keep drying and test again.
If the salt stays loose and falls freely, the grain is dry enough for storage in most cases. A moisture meter, if your group or buyer has one, gives an exact reading.
Cleaning and grading

Cleaning means removing stones, chaff, cob pieces, broken grains, insects and any mouldy or discoloured grain by winnowing and sieving. **Grading** means sorting produce into groups of similar quality so a buyer knows exactly what they are getting. For tomatoes, grades usually follow ripeness, size and damage: firm, evenly coloured, unbruised fruit in one group; smaller or slightly marked fruit in another; soft or split fruit for immediate local use or processing.
Worked example: does sorting tomatoes pay?
For example, Grace has 30 crates of tomatoes. A trader offers ₦14,000 per crate for the mixed lot. These are illustrative prices.
Grace sorts them: 18 crates Grade A, 9 crates Grade B, 3 crates Grade C (soft, for immediate sale).
Prices offered after sorting: Grade A ₦18,000, Grade B ₦13,000, Grade C ₦6,000 to local soup sellers.
She paid two helpers ₦4,000 each for half a day of sorting: ₦8,000.
Net gain from grading: ₦39,000 − ₦8,000 = ₦31,000.
Grading added ₦31,000 to one load. It also stopped soft fruit from spoiling the good fruit, and gave her a reputation for honest Grade A crates.
Packaging that cuts losses

**Fresh produce:** stackable, ventilated plastic crates protect tomatoes and pepper far better than overfilled raffia baskets, which crush the fruit at the bottom. Do not overfill, keep crates in shade, and load trucks so crates do not slide.
**Grain:** use clean, new or well-washed bags. Old fertiliser or chemical bags must never be used for food.
**Hermetic (airtight) storage bags**, such as triple-layer PICS bags, seal out air so insects die without chemical insecticides. Grain must be dry before sealing.
**Labels:** write your name or group, crop, grade, weight and date on each bag or crate. It builds trust and helps you trace any complaint.
ear-of-maize
An ear of maize
Clean, dry, graded maize is what feed mills and serious buyers pay a premium for.
Handling fresh produce

Fresh crops lose quality by the hour once they are picked. Harvest tomatoes and pepper in the cool early morning, put them in the shade straight away and handle them gently, as every drop and squeeze leaves a bruise that rots later. For long journeys, pick tomatoes when they are just starting to change colour rather than fully red, so they ripen on the way instead of arriving soft. Do not pack produce wet, and travel in the cooler part of the day or at night where it is safe.
Storage chemicals can kill

Never keep grain storage tablets such as aluminium phosphide (often sold as fumigant tablets) in or near your home, and never use them yourself. They release a very poisonous gas and have caused deaths in households. Fumigation should only be done by trained, licensed operators. Choose hermetic bags or approved methods advised by your extension officer, follow every label, and keep all farm chemicals locked away from food and children.
Dry grain on a tarpaulin, not bare ground, to about 13% moisture for maize before storage.
The salt-in-a-bottle test is a free way to check whether grain is still too wet.
Grading separates quality so buyers pay more for your best produce.
Crates, clean bags and hermetic bags reduce losses; never reuse chemical bags for food.
Leave fumigation with aluminium phosphide to licensed operators only.

Clean and sort the batch into two or three grades and weigh or count each grade.
Label each bag or crate with crop, grade, weight and date.

Food Safety and Buyer Quality Standards: Aflatoxin, Pesticide Residues and Fair Weighing
Explain what aflatoxin is, where it comes from and how to prevent it
Follow pesticide label rules, including the waiting period before harvest
Read a buyer's quality specification and prepare produce to meet it
Make sure women in the household and group are paid and recognised fairly

Better buyers check quality because their own customers, regulators and reputation depend on it. Meeting their standards is not just about appearance. Two hidden problems matter most for health and for price: **aflatoxin** in stored grains and nuts, and **pesticide residues** on fresh produce. This lesson explains both, then shows you how to read a buyer's specification and weigh fairly.
Aflatoxin: the invisible danger in mouldy grain

Aflatoxins are poisons produced by certain moulds (mainly Aspergillus species) that grow on crops such as maize, groundnuts and other grains and nuts, especially when they are damaged, poorly dried or stored in warm, damp conditions. The World Health Organization identifies aflatoxins as a serious health risk: large doses can cause acute poisoning and long-term exposure is linked to liver cancer. Normal cooking does not reliably destroy them, so prevention is the only real protection.
Harvest on time; do not leave mature crops standing in the rain.
Avoid damaging grain and pods during harvesting and shelling, because broken grain moulds faster.
Dry quickly and thoroughly on tarpaulins, as in the previous lesson.
Sort out and remove mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured grain and nuts.
Store in clean, dry, raised and well-ventilated places or in hermetic bags.
Ask your ADP extension officer about Aflasafe, a biocontrol product developed with IITA that is applied in the field to reduce aflatoxin-producing moulds.
Do not sell or feed mouldy grain

Grain that is visibly mouldy should not be sold for food, eaten at home or fed to animals, since aflatoxin passes into animals and can reach milk. Mixing mouldy grain into a good lot to hide it is dishonest and dangerous, and it can get your whole lot rejected by a buyer who tests.
Pesticides: follow the label, every time

Every registered pesticide label states the dose, the protective clothing needed and the **pre-harvest interval**: the number of days you must wait between the last spray and harvest. Harvesting earlier leaves residues on the produce. Buyers who supply supermarkets or export may test for residues. Wear gloves, a mask and long sleeves when spraying, never spray into the wind, wash hands before eating, and never store chemicals in food or drink containers.
Quality checks a buyer may make
Moisture content
Foreign matter and stones
Broken or damaged grain
Mould and discolouration
Insect damage
Correct weight
Prepare for each check before the buyer arrives and you avoid rejected bags and price cuts.
Reading a buyer's specification

Processors and institutional buyers usually give a written **specification**: the quality limits they accept. Ask for it in writing before you deliver. It may set a maximum moisture level, a maximum share of foreign matter or broken grain, a colour or variety, or a ripeness stage for tomatoes. If you do not understand a term, ask the buyer or your extension officer to explain it. If your produce cannot meet the specification, agree in advance what happens to the bags that fail.
Worked example: do plastic crates pay back?

For example, Halima sells about 40 loads of tomatoes a season. Her own records show she lost about 20% to crushing in raffia baskets. A group member using crates reports losses of about 5%. Prices are approximate.
Losses with raffia baskets: 20% of 40 loads = 8 loads.
Expected losses with crates: 5% of 40 loads = 2 loads.
Loads saved: 8 − 2 = 6 loads. At about ₦15,000 per load, that is 6 × ₦15,000 = ₦90,000 saved per season.
She buys 20 plastic crates at about ₦5,000 each: 20 × ₦5,000 = ₦100,000.
Payback: ₦100,000 ÷ ₦90,000 = about 1.1 seasons.
The crates pay for themselves in just over one season and can be reused for several more, so every later season adds roughly ₦90,000. Halima also gets a better price because her tomatoes arrive firm.

Fair weighing and inclusion

Local measures such as the **mudu**, the basket or the "big bag" vary in size from market to market, which makes prices hard to compare and easy to cheat on. Where you can, weigh in kilograms on a scale you can see. A farmer group can buy one good scale for everyone to share. Women often do much of the drying, sorting and selling work. Make sure that women's names appear on group records and contracts, and that their payments go into their own bank or mobile money accounts, so their work is recognised and the income reaches them.
Moving into processing

Raw produce sold in bulk is handled differently from processed, packaged food. If you start selling packaged products such as garri, flour or ground pepper with your own label, NAFDAC registration and labelling rules apply. Check current requirements on the NAFDAC website or at a NAFDAC office before you start.

Sales Records, Price per Kilogram and Measuring Your Gains
Convert prices in different units to naira per kilogram
Keep a simple sales record on paper or in Google Sheets
Calculate net income per kilogram before and after an improvement
Use your records to decide what to keep doing next season

You have learned to grade, pack and meet buyer standards. Now you need proof that these changes paid. Feelings such as "things went better this year" are not enough, because prices change with the season. A simple record of every sale, converted to the same unit, shows you clearly what worked.
Step one: one unit for every price

Buyers quote in different units: a 100 kg bag, a 50 kg bag, a basket, a mudu. To compare, convert everything to **naira per kilogram**. Divide the price by the weight in kilograms. If you sell by a local measure, weigh a few filled measures on a scale and use the average weight.
Worked example: which offer is really best?
For example, Ngozi has three offers for her soybeans. Prices are illustrative.
Buyer A: ₦62,000 per 100 kg bag. Price per kg = 62,000 ÷ 100 = ₦620.
Buyer B: ₦32,500 per 50 kg bag. Price per kg = 32,500 ÷ 50 = ₦650.
Market retail: ₦900 per mudu. Ngozi weighs five full mudu and gets 6.5 kg in total, so one mudu is 6.5 ÷ 5 = 1.3 kg. Price per kg = 900 ÷ 1.3 = about ₦692.
But retail sales are slow: she sells only about 40 kg a day and pays ₦1,000 transport each market day, which is 1,000 ÷ 40 = ₦25 per kg. Net is about ₦667 per kg.
Buyer B at ₦650 per kg takes the whole lot in one day.

Retail gives the highest price per kg but takes many days. Buyer B beats Buyer A by ₦30 per kg, which on 2,000 kg is ₦60,000. Without converting, "₦62,000 a bag" sounds better than "₦32,500 a bag" when it is not.

When to Sell: Storage, Seasonal Prices and the Break-Even Price for Waiting
Explain why prices for many crops are usually lowest just after harvest
Calculate the break-even future price that makes storage worth it
List the costs and risks of storing, including money tied up
Plan to sell in batches instead of all at once

For storable crops such as maize, sorghum, millet, soybeans, beans and rice, prices often follow the season. Just after harvest, almost everyone is selling and many need cash quickly, so supply is high and prices tend to be at their lowest. Months later, in the lean season before the next harvest, stocks are smaller and prices tend to rise. A farmer who can store well and wait may earn more. But the rise is **never guaranteed**: imports, government releases from reserves, a good harvest elsewhere or many farmers storing at once can keep prices flat or push them down.
Sell at harvest or store and sell later
Sell at harvest
Store and sell later
Cash immediately
No storage costs
No storage losses
Usually the lowest price
Possible higher price
Bags and storage cost money
Risk of insects and mould
Money tied up for months
Storage is a business decision with costs and risks, not a free way to earn more.
The costs of waiting
**Storage materials:** hermetic bags, pallets to keep bags off the floor, or a share of a warehouse fee.
**Losses:** some weight loss and damage, even in good storage; much more in poor storage.
**Money tied up:** if you must borrow to cover household needs while you wait, the interest is a storage cost. If you do not borrow, you still give up what that money could have done.
**Risk:** prices might not rise, and theft or fire are possible. Store in a secure, dry place.
Worked example: is it worth storing 20 bags of maize for four months?
For example, Fatima has 20 bags of well-dried maize (100 kg each). These numbers are illustrative.
To store, she buys 20 hermetic bags at about ₦2,500 each: ₦50,000.
She would need to borrow ₦300,000 for school fees at 5% per month: 4 × 5% × ₦300,000 = ₦60,000 interest.
She expects losses of about 2% even in good storage: 2% of 20 bags = 0.4 bags, leaving 19.6 bags to sell.
If the price in four months is ₦70,000: 19.6 × ₦70,000 = ₦1,372,000. Minus ₦50,000 bags and ₦60,000 interest = ₦1,262,000, which is ₦162,000 more than selling now.
If the price is only ₦58,000: 19.6 × ₦58,000 = ₦1,136,800, minus ₦110,000 = ₦1,026,800, which is ₦73,200 less than selling now.

Storage only pays if the future price is clearly above about ₦61,700. Fatima decides to sell 8 bags now to cover school fees without a loan and store 12, which removes the interest cost and halves her risk.
How to decide
Check your grain is dry (about 13% or less for maize) and clean before storing; poor grain should be sold, not stored.
Collect price history: ask traders, your ADP extension office or experienced farmers what prices did in the same months over the last two or three years.
Calculate your break-even future price as in the example.
Store only if the likely price is well above break-even and you can cope if it is not.
Sell in batches: some at harvest for urgent needs, the rest in two or three lots over the following months.
Inspect stored bags every few weeks for insects, damp or bad smells.
tear-off-calendar
A tear-off calendar
Timing your sales across the months can matter as much as choosing the buyer.
Warehouse and commodity exchange options

In parts of Nigeria, private warehouse operators and commodity exchanges accept graded grain from farmers, store it and give a receipt that can sometimes be used to access credit or to sell later. Terms, fees and quality rules differ. Read the terms carefully, ask other farmers about their experience, and confirm the company is properly registered before depositing produce.
Keeping stored grain safe
Store bags on wooden pallets, not directly on the floor, and a little away from walls so air moves and damp does not soak in.
With hermetic bags, fill with dry grain, squeeze out as much air as you can, and twist and tie each inner layer separately before tying the outer bag.
Keep sealed bags in shade and protect them from rats, which can chew holes and break the seal; set traps and keep the store clean.
Do not open hermetic bags often; each opening lets air back in.
Mark each bag with the date stored, so the oldest grain is sold first.

Be careful with price rumours. A neighbour saying that maize will "double by June" is not evidence. Base your expectation on what prices actually did in past years, and remember that past patterns are a guide, not a promise.
Fresh produce does not wait

Tomatoes, pepper and leafy vegetables cannot be stored for months without cold storage or processing. For these crops, timing means planting so that harvest falls when supply is lower, and selling quickly while quality is high.
Storable crop prices are often lowest at harvest and higher in the lean season, but never guaranteed.
Break-even future price = (value now + storage costs + interest) ÷ units left after losses.
Store only dry, clean grain, and only if the likely price is well above break-even.
Selling in batches spreads risk and reduces the need to borrow.

Group Marketing, Cooperatives and Written Buyer Agreements
Explain how bulking produce with other farmers opens better channels
Calculate the gain per farmer from shared transport and a better price
List the key terms a written buyer agreement should include
Prepare your walk-away option before negotiating, and spot fake buyer scams

Many processors, wholesalers and institutional buyers will not deal with a farmer who has five or ten bags. They want a full truckload, a steady supply and one contact person. A group of farmers who bulk their produce together can meet those needs, share transport, buy inputs and storage bags in bulk, and negotiate with more confidence. This is called **collective** or **group marketing**.
Steps up in market power
Formal buyer agreement
Registered cooperative
Organised farmer group
Individual farmer
Each step up adds volume, trust and bargaining power; most groups start informally and formalise as they grow.
Worked example: twelve women fill one truck
For example, twelve women in a village savings group in Kwara State each have 10 bags of maize (120 bags in total). A feed mill buys a minimum of 100 bags per delivery. Prices are illustrative.
Farm gate price: ₦55,000 per bag.
Mill price: ₦66,000 per bag, delivered.
Truck hire to the mill for the full load: ₦360,000. Per bag: ₦360,000 ÷ 120 = ₦3,000.
The group sets aside ₦500 per bag for loading, the scale and the record keeper's airtime.
Gain per bag over farm gate = ₦62,500 − ₦55,000 = ₦7,500.

No single woman could have filled the truck, but together they earned ₦75,000 each more than at the farm gate. This only works if every bag meets the mill's moisture and cleanliness standard, so the group checks every member's bags before loading.
Making a group work
Agree simple written rules: who can join, quality standards for bags, how costs are shared, how money is paid out.
Choose a treasurer and a record keeper, and record each member's bags by weight and grade.
Pay each member directly into her own account, with a written statement of her bags, price and deductions.
Hold a short meeting after each sale to share results openly.
As you grow, consider registering as a cooperative with your state's department of cooperatives, which gives legal recognition and can help with bank accounts, loans and formal contracts.
What a written buyer agreement should include
Term
What to agree
Parties
Full names, addresses and phone numbers of the group and the buyer
Product and quality
Crop, variety or grade, and the specification (for example maximum moisture)
Quantity
Number of bags or kg, and delivery dates
Price
Fixed price per kg or bag, or a clear formula such as the market price on delivery day
Weighing
Where, on whose scale, and that a group member witnesses it
Payment
Method, account name and number, and the number of days after delivery
Rejection
How rejected bags are handled and who pays transport back
Disputes
Who the parties will go to first if there is a disagreement
Negotiate from your best alternative

Before any negotiation, know your **walk-away option**: what you will do if this deal fails, for example the weekly market price you calculated, minus costs. Negotiation experts call this your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If a buyer's offer is below your walk-away option and below your minimum price from Module 1, you can say no politely and confidently.
handshake-deal
Two people shaking hands on a deal
A handshake is a start, but a written agreement protects both the group and the buyer.
Running a fair delivery day
Two days before, the quality team checks every member's bags for moisture, cleanliness and weight, and sets aside bags that fail.
On the day, weigh each member's bags with the member present and write the weights in the group book.
Give each member a slip showing her number of bags, total kg and grade.
At the buyer, a group representative witnesses the weighing and collects a signed delivery note.
When payment arrives, the treasurer shares a statement showing the price, total deductions and each member's amount before paying each one into her own account.

The biggest threat to group selling is **side-selling**: a member who promised bags to the group's contract sells them to a passing trader for quick cash. The group then cannot fill the order and the buyer loses trust. Agree in advance what happens if a member cannot deliver, and consider small cash advances from group savings for members in urgent need, so they are not forced to side-sell.
Fake buyers and off-taker scams

Be suspicious of any buyer who asks your group to pay a "registration", "membership" or "processing" fee before they buy, promises prices far above the market, or will only communicate by WhatsApp. Look up a company's registration on the CAC public search (search.cac.gov.ng), ask for references from other farmers, visit their premises if you can, and never release produce until payment is confirmed in your own account.
Bulking with other farmers unlocks buyers who need full loads and shares transport costs.
Groups succeed with written rules, honest records and direct payment to each member.
A written agreement covers quality, quantity, price, weighing, payment, rejection and disputes.
Know your walk-away option before negotiating, and never pay a fee to be allowed to sell.

Your Market Access Improvement Project and 90-Day Plan

This final lesson brings everything together into your **Market Access Improvement Project**. It has three parts: proof from your own produce that grading and packaging change your price, a comparison of at least two buyer options beyond your usual one, and a 90-day plan to keep improving. It should be about your real farm and your real numbers, not general ideas.
Part 1: before-and-after price comparison

Use your sales record from Module 2. Take one lot sold the usual way and one lot that you dried, cleaned, graded and packed properly. Convert both to net naira per kilogram. Note the date of each sale and, if you can, the general market price on each day, so you can show the improvement is more than a seasonal price change. Include photos of your graded produce and labels.
Part 2: compare at least two buyer options
List possible buyers: a feed mill or processor, a wholesaler in a bigger market, a school, hotel or caterer, a supermarket supplier, a warehouse or commodity exchange.
Phone or visit each and ask the six channel questions from Module 1: quality, quantity, weighing, payment, rejection and repeat business.
Ask for their written specification if they have one.
Calculate the net price per kg for each option after transport and other selling costs.
Check each buyer: CAC registration where relevant, references from other farmers, and their payment record.
Worked example: Ngozi's project summary
For example, Ngozi grows maize in Benue State. Her numbers are illustrative to show the format.
Before: 10 bags sold mixed at the farm gate at ₦52,000 per 100 kg bag = ₦520 per kg net.
After: 10 bags dried, cleaned, graded and in clean new bags, sold at the weekly market at ₦60,000 per bag. Selling costs ₦2,000 per bag. Net = ₦58,000 per bag = ₦580 per kg.
Improvement: ₦580 − ₦520 = ₦60 per kg, or ₦6,000 per bag. On 10 bags that is ₦60,000.
She paid ₦8,000 for tarpaulin use and helpers, so net gain = ₦60,000 − ₦8,000 = ₦52,000.
Option comparison: feed mill net ₦610 per kg but needs 100 bags and pays in 14 days; a poultry farmer nearby nets ₦590 per kg, buys 20 bags a month and pays on delivery.
Ngozi shows a clear ₦60 per kg improvement and chooses the poultry farmer for steady monthly sales while organising neighbours to fill a mill truck next season.
